fullText:
Can we predict electronic bands beyond DFT across different systems?

A material’s electronic band structure provides the basis for band gaps, densities of states, and carrier effective masses, while connecting theory with spectroscopy. For quantum materials, getting these bands right can change our understanding of physics. Yet the calculations needed to go beyond standard DFT remain expensive.

We introduce O-krystal, a periodic E(3)-equivariant graph neural network that learns corrections to individual electronic states. It uses orbital information from lower cost PBE calculations in both real and reciprocal space, bringing local electronic interactions and the momentum dependence of the crystal into the same model.

O-kRystal is the first machine learning framework to combine:

1. Scale across chemistry: HSE06 band predictions across nearly 6,000 chemically diverse three dimensional materials

2. Breadth across electronic behavior: metals and insulators, magnetic and nonmagnetic systems, with spin resolution and different numbers of bands

3. Flexibility across theory and dimensionality: the same framework, trained separately, predicts G0W0 quasiparticle energies in two dimensional materials.

Although trained only at high symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs densities of states from dense Brillouin zone predictions.

On a separate benchmark of strongly correlated materials, O-kRystal reduces the PBE band energy MAE by 68.7%. As demonstrated for AFM-II MnO, a canonical Mott insulator, it captures distinct corrections to Mn 3d and O 2p states, recovering their relative placement by accounting for the effects of exact exchange.

As electronic structure methods advance, this framework offers a path toward experimental accuracy and large-scale discovery of quantum materials with emergent phases, including superconductivity. @Caltech

Great application of small language models from Salesforce and colleagues.

AI-scientist pipelines are well known to struggle to propose novel and diverse research ideas.

This team trains an 8B reasoning model to write several research ideas in one generation from a set of source papers.

The reward scores the whole set, weighting each idea's quality by how far it sits from the ideas written before it. The model learns to move each new idea away from the earlier ones.

On their contamination-free benchmark, the 8B model scores higher on creative utility, a measure that combines quality and diversity, than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra.

fullText:
A 3B-active model can now write long-term memory as well as Claude Opus 5.

Tencent Hunyuan trained Hy-Memory-30B-A3B for one job. It decides what an agent stores, how precisely, and how new evidence updates what is already there.

The same model runs inside Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, it ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average against 54.62% for Opus 5.

Training has two stages. On-policy distillation teaches each framework's write protocol. RL then rewards the writer when later questions can be answered from what it stored, with a penalty for storing too much.

fullText:
Some observations about the "total" automation of software engineering:

1. There are more software engineers now than in 2025, and demand is growing.

2. Software engineers have never worked harder than they do now.

3. They largely don't write code anymore, agents write ~100% of the code.

4. The bottom line of the companies that employs these engineers and agents (i.e. the terminal purpose of all this code) is typically not budging as a result of AI adoption.

This is why you have to think in terms of systems. Automating one aspect of a system creates its own friction and moves the bottlenecks elsewhere.

fullText:
Ali Ghodsi of @Databricks on the four conditions that would have to hold for AI to truly improve itself:

"The next model requires less resources, less GPUs to train... The second condition: the next model takes less time to train as well. Third, accuracy of the model, the intelligence is increasing. And fourth, we can do the former three again and again and again... All at the same time, not just any of them."

"If you just mean that the software is writing itself, we're already there today. Like 90-some percent of the software in Databricks is written by AI. Does it matter if the last few percent is also written by AI? No."

"If you're getting these four conditions, then you might get a speed-up where the next model, let's say, takes half amount of time and half the resources, and it is more intelligent... By the way, I don't even know if that necessarily leads you to superintelligence."

"A lot of people, their definition is just, 'Hey, if I'm not even coding anymore and it's coding itself'... I think they're conflating, 'Hey, what's my value and is it scary for me?' Versus, 'Hey, that then means we'll get that superintelligence that in 2014 was hypothesized by Bostrom.'"

@alighodsi @martin_casado @sarah_wang

fullText:
Last year I thought Threads was an existential risk to X. 

When Meta puts its full weight behind something -- by injecting the app into Instagram, it’s DEFCON 5:

You have to squeeze out every last drop of growth from all available surfaces to save the app.

However, I started to realize that the opposite was happening:

It was strengthening X.

If you look at any announcement by Zuck, you will see the most rude & toxic comments on the internet. 

But when he makes those same announcements on X, people are thrilled about how he’s pushing humanity forward. X is a place where people are excited about the future, so it’s no surprise he and his top lieutenants are using it more than their own app.

Threads — and Bluesky — have effectively quarantined some of the worst people on the internet. 

And so I had an epiphany: those apps are X’s anti-abuse systems.
